html:
Human babies are famously born completely helpless. Unable to even hold their heads up on their own, they rely on nearby humans for food, water, and the rest of their needs. That makes figuring out who can be counted on to provide those things pretty important for the little guys. According to a new study published in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior, they might accomplish this important goal by watching who swaps spit. 

“We were inspired by studies that found that across cultures, people in close relationships are often more comfortable sharing saliva with each other,” study author Brandon Woo of the University of California, Santa Barbara explained in a statement. “So imagine seeing two people licking the same ice cream cone—could you guess how they might know each other?”

I could, but could a 4- to 6-month-old baby? 

To find out, Woo and fellow psychologists from Harvard and MIT got their hands on some infants and treated them to a series of experimental puppet shows. In the first, an adult placed an orange slice in their mouth and then in the mouth of a puppet—a clear representation of saliva sharing. The team then had another adult pass a ball to the puppet to represent sharing without the spit. 

Read more: “Do Babies Feel Shame?”

In the next act of the production, the puppet expressed distress. The researchers monitored the infants to see which person (orange-sharer or ball-passer) they looked to as a signifier of which relationship they deemed closer, which is common in other primates. In studies of vervet monkeys, for example, juveniles will look to the mother of another juvenile if it emits a distress call. 

The cast of the next puppet show included two puppet actors and a single human. It was also food-free. Instead of oranges, a human put their finger in their mouth, placed it in one puppet’s mouth, and then back in their own. They subsequently touched their forehead, touched the second puppet’s forehead, and then their own. After that bit of character development, the human protagonist acted like they were crying while the researchers watched which puppet the babies looked to. 

“The first experiment focuses on a very familiar action: food sharing,” Woo explained. “The second behavior, with the finger in someone’s mouth versus someone else’s mouth, is not as common in children’s everyday lives.” (Hey, let’s hope so.)

The team found that in both scenarios, infants favored the saliva-sharers over the ball-passers or the forehead-touchers. Put simply, it seems the little tots inferred a certain closeness in the relationship of those who swapped spit. 

It’s not the first time researchers have discovered babies making this inference, but it’s the first time in infants this young. The team performed the same experiment on babies between the ages of 8 and 10 months as part of another study. By that age, 90 percent of babies are being fed solid food and are probably more familiar with witnessing the intimate behavior of saliva sharing, which means it may be learned. But between the age of 4 and 6 months, only around half of babies have started eating solid food. 

In other words, these findings suggest representations of close social relationships could be part of a baby’s core knowledge, or the factory-installed firmware they’re born with. “It’s really cool that babies are still making inferences in both cases. That even with less familiar actions they’re making inferences about closeness,” Woo said. “It’s fascinating that they seem to have this abstract knowledge about relationships that applies across different actions.”
